name: Visser Thin Shell Wormhole
description: Matt Visser's traversable wormhole of 1989: two copies of the Schwarzschild exterior cut at a radius $a$ outside the horizon and joined there. All of its matter is a thin shell of negative surface energy density at the throat, and everywhere else spacetime is vacuum.
convention: The Schwarzschild radius is $r_s = 2GM/c^2$, and we keep factors of $c$ explicit. The Ricci tensor is the standard contraction, $R_{\mu\nu} = R^\alpha{}_{\mu\alpha\nu}$.

coordinates.name: Schwarzschild

parameters.description: Schwarzschild radius, $r_s = 2GM/c^2$, with $M$ the mass seen from either side
Throat radius, $a > r_s$, the areal radius at which the two exteriors are joined

coordinates.convention: We use coordinates $(t, r, \theta, \phi)$ on either side of the throat, with $t$ carrying dimensions of time and $r$ the areal radius. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.

coordinates.name: Through the Throat

parameters.description: Schwarzschild radius, $r_s = 2GM/c^2$, with $M$ the mass seen from either side
Throat radius, $a > r_s$, the areal radius at which the two exteriors are joined

coordinates.convention: We use coordinates $(t, \ell, \theta, \phi)$, with $t$ carrying dimensions of time and the length $\ell = r - a$ on one side of the throat and $a - r$ on the other, and $\delta$ is the Dirac delta. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.

history: Michael Morris and Kip Thorne showed in 1988 that the throat of a wormhole a person could cross must hold a radial tension $\tau_0$ greater than its energy density $\rho_0c^2$, and wrote that "No known material has this $\tau_0 > \rho_0c^2$ property" [morris1988]. Matt Visser gave examples in 1989 that "in some sense minimize the use of exotic matter" [visser1989prd]. He cut identical regions out of two copies of Minkowski space and identified their boundaries, so that the matter sits only on the join, with a negative surface energy density and a negative tension where the region removed is convex [visser1989prd]. With a sharp cornered cube removed, the matter gathers on its edges as a string of negative tension, and a traveller crossing a flat face "will feel no tidal forces and see no matter, exotic or otherwise" [visser1989prd].¶In the same year Visser removed the region $r \le a$ from two copies of the Schwarzschild spacetime and identified the two spheres $r = a$, joining two asymptotically flat universes at a throat [visser1989nuclphysb]. The throat has to lie outside the horizon, $a > r_s$, a condition "necessary to prevent the formation of an event horizon" [visser1989nuclphysb]. Off the throat the spacetime is piecewise Schwarzschild, so the stress energy vanishes everywhere except on the throat, where it is proportional to a delta function [visser1989nuclphysb]. Visser counted these wormholes among the "absurdly benign" ones of Morris and Thorne, in the limit where the layer of exotic matter shrinks to zero thickness [visser1989nuclphysb, morris1988].¶The junction conditions of a thin shell fix its surface stress energy by the jump in extrinsic curvature across it [poisson1995]. Nikhilranjan Sen wrote the boundary conditions of the gravitational field at a surface of discontinuity in 1924, and Kornel Lanczos the field of matter spread over a surface the same year [sen1924, lanczos1924shell]. Werner Israel recast the conditions in 1966 in terms of the extrinsic curvature alone, with no mention of coordinates [israel1966]. On Visser's throat they give the surface energy density $\sigma = -(c^4/2\pi Ga)\sqrt{1 - r_s/a}$ and the surface pressure $p = (c^4/4\pi Ga)(1 - r_s/2a)/\sqrt{1 - r_s/a}$ [visser1989nuclphysb, poisson1995]. Visser read the negative energy density as a special case of the defocusing argument by which Morris and Thorne had inferred exotic matter at the throat of every traversable wormhole [visser1989nuclphysb, morris1988]. The pressure is positive, and it holds the throat against collapse [visser1989nuclphysb].¶The whole of the matter sits on one sphere, so the radius of the throat obeys a single equation of motion, that of a particle in a potential [visser1989nuclphysb, poisson1995]. From it Visser found in 1989 that a throat made of a classical membrane, whose energy density equals its tension, is dynamically unstable [visser1989nuclphysb]. Eric Poisson and Visser characterised the exotic matter near a static throat in 1995 by $\beta^2 = dp/d\sigma$, and found the throat stable against radial perturbations only for $\beta^2$ above a positive bound when it lies inside the photon sphere $a = 3r_s/2$, and below a negative bound when it lies outside [poisson1995]. Stability therefore needs $\beta^2$ outside the range from $0$ to $c^2$ of the square of a speed of sound, and Poisson and Visser noted that without a microphysical model of the exotic matter "there is no guarantee that $\beta_0$ actually is the speed of sound" [poisson1995].¶Mustapha Ishak and Kayll Lake carried the analysis of thin shells and wormholes over to spacetimes with a cosmological constant in 2002 [ishak2002]. Francisco Lobo and Paulo Crawford found in 2004 that a large positive cosmological constant, the Schwarzschild-de Sitter case, enlarges the region of stability Poisson and Visser had found, and that a negative one shrinks it [lobo2004crawford]. For charged thin shell wormholes, Ernesto Eiroa and Gustavo Romero showed the same year that a large charge makes the constraints on the equation of state less severe [eiroa2004]. Nadiezhda Montelongo Garcia, Lobo and Visser showed in 2012 for every spherically symmetric thin shell wormhole that its stability "is equivalent to choosing suitable properties for the exotic material residing on the wormhole throat" [garcia2012].¶A throat inside the photon sphere violates the weak energy condition and satisfies the null and strong ones [cardoso2016prl]. Vitor Cardoso, Edgardo Franzin and Paolo Pani put the throat there in 2016, at $a = r_s + \ell$ with $\ell$ much smaller than $r_s$, and dropped a particle radially through it [cardoso2016prl]. The first ringdown they found is that of a Schwarzschild black hole of the same mass, although the quasinormal modes of the wormhole are completely different, since the ringdown is set by the light ring [cardoso2016prl]. The wormhole's own modes appear only after a delay growing as $\ln(r_s/\ell)$, about sixteen damping times of the black hole's fundamental mode for a final mass of 60 solar masses even with $\ell$ at the Planck length [cardoso2016prl]. Cardoso, Seth Hopper, Caio Macedo, Carlos Palenzuela and Pani showed later in 2016 that the late signal is a train of "echoes" of the modes of the photon sphere, reflected between the two peaks of the potential, one at the light ring on each side [cardoso2016prd].¶Jahed Abedi, Hannah Dykaar and Niayesh Afshordi searched the LIGO data of three black hole merger events for such echoes in 2016, and reported tentative evidence at a false detection probability of 1%, published in 2017 [abedi2017]. Julian Westerweck and his collaborators repeated the analysis in 2018, found a lower significance "entirely consistent with noise", and concluded that it gave no observational evidence of structure at the horizon [westerweck2018]. In 2021 the LIGO and Virgo collaborations searched 31 binary black hole signals of their second catalogue with a template built on the model of Abedi and his collaborators, and found no statistically significant evidence of echoes [abbott2021tgr]. The LIGO, Virgo and KAGRA collaborations reported in 2025 that they found none either in their third catalogue, with a search independent of the shape of the signal [abbott2025tgr].
